summary: Stepping back to synthesize the broader picture, the standoff between fixed income and risk assets has reached an untenable extreme. For weeks, the market operated on the thesis that robust nominal G.D.P. growth would allow corporate balance sheets to outgrow rising borrowing costs.

Stepping back to synthesize the broader picture, today’s action deepens the standoff between fixed income and risk assets that has defined trading all month. For weeks, the market operated on the comfortable thesis that nominal G.D.P. growth would let corporate balance sheets easily outgrow rising capital costs. But that thesis breaks down when Treasury yields clear five percent and stay there.

Stepping back to synthesize the broader picture, today’s market action deepens the regime standoff we have tracked throughout September. Equities spent weeks trying to look through elevated capital costs on the thesis that nominal revenue growth would insulate margins. But when ten-year paper clears five percent and heads toward five-twenty, that thesis breaks down.

Stepping back to synthesize the broader picture, today’s action represents the long-awaited collision between our two running themes: the macro regime standoff and balance sheet physics. For most of September, risk assets operated under the convenient fiction that nominal G.D.P. growth would effortlessly outrun capital costs.

Stepping back to synthesize the broader picture, today’s action represents the continuation of our core running theme: the collision between the macro regime standoff and balance sheet physics. For weeks, risk assets operated under the convenient fiction that nominal G.D.P. growth would effortlessly outrun capital costs.

Stepping back to synthesize the broader picture, today’s action represents the continuation of our core running theme: the violent friction between the macro regime standoff and balance sheet physics. For weeks, risk assets operated under the comfortable fiction that nominal G.D.P. growth would effortlessly outrun capital costs.

Stepping back to synthesize the broader picture, today’s action represents an aggressive acceleration of the regime standoff we have tracked over recent sessions. The convenient fiction that nominal revenue growth would effortlessly bail out corporate debt structures simply fails when ten-year paper anchors comfortably above five and a quarter percent.
